item.title: Ableton Live
item.description:
It includes instruments, effects, and MIDI tools, plus Max for Live for building custom devices. Newer versions offer stem separation and other assisted features. Live runs on Windows and macOS.

It is sold in several editions at different prices.

Logic Pro and FL Studio are alternatives. Ableton Live suits music producers who perform or work in loops.

item.title: Audacity
item.description:
It records from microphones, edits waveforms, and applies effects such as noise reduction and compression. Plug-ins extend it, and there are AI-based plug-ins for noise and transcription.

It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. It is destructive in some workflows, so keep copies of originals.

Adobe Audition and Reaper are alternatives. Audacity suits narrators and podcasters who need a free editor.

item.title: Axon Draft One
item.description:
The system transcribes the recording and produces a first-person narrative in a standard report format. Officers must check facts, correct errors, and attest to the final report. Some agencies add flags that mark AI-drafted text.

It is sold to agencies, and some jurisdictions and prosecutors have set rules on its use.

Transcription tools such as Truleo and Rev serve related needs. Axon Draft One suits police officers who write many reports.

item.title: Dext
item.description:
Clients photograph a receipt or forward an invoice by email, and Dext reads the supplier, date, amount, and tax. The extracted data syncs to platforms such as Xero, QuickBooks, and Sage, where it becomes a draft transaction ready for review. It can also fetch supplier bills automatically.

Practices use it to collect documents from many clients in one place and spend less time keying numbers. Extraction is good but not perfect, so someone still checks unusual or poorly scanned documents.

item.title: FFmpeg
item.description:
Broadcast engineers and developers use it to transcode feeds, create proxies, and automate batch tasks. Many video apps use it behind the scenes. Recent versions can run Whisper-based transcription.

It runs from the command line, so there is a learning curve.

HandBrake offers a simpler interface for conversion. FFmpeg suits engineers who automate media workflows.

item.title: FL Studio
item.description:
The pattern-based step sequencer and piano roll make it quick to sketch ideas. It comes with synths, samplers, and effects, and includes stem separation. Image-Line has a lifetime free updates policy.

Editions differ by feature set and price.

Ableton Live and Logic Pro are alternatives. FL Studio suits producers who start from beats.

item.title: Logic Pro
item.description:
It includes a large library of instruments and loops, plus tools like Session Players, which generate drummer, bass, and keyboard parts. Stem splitter separates tracks from mixed audio. Dolby Atmos mixing is supported.

It is a one-time purchase on Mac and a subscription on iPad.

Ableton Live and FL Studio are alternatives. Logic Pro suits musicians in the Apple ecosystem.

item.title: Praat
item.description:
Users load recordings, view spectrograms, annotate segments, and run scripts for batch analysis. It also supports speech synthesis experiments. The interface is old-fashioned but very capable.

It is open source and runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

ELAN is useful for annotating video and audio. Praat suits linguists studying phonetics.

item.title: Pro Tools
item.description:
It handles multitrack recording, comping, and large session management. Surround and Dolby Atmos mixing are supported. It works with Avid and third-party interfaces and plug-ins, and has added assisted features such as stem separation.

It is sold by subscription or perpetual license, with a free entry version.

Logic Pro and Reaper are alternatives. Pro Tools suits sound engineers in professional studios.

item.title: Amazon Textract
item.description: Textract turns images of documents into structured data. A developer sends a scanned file or PDF, and the service returns the text it finds along with its layout: it identifies tables and preserves their rows and columns, detects key-value pairs in forms such as a name field and its value, and recognizes handwriting. This is much more useful than plain text recognition, which would return an unordered block of characters.

item.title: Apple Vision Pro
item.description:
Vision Pro puts a computer in front of your eyes. High-resolution displays and cameras show the real world with digital windows and objects placed in it, and you interact by looking at things and pinching your fingers, with no controllers needed. It runs visionOS and supports iPad and Apple apps, along with apps made for spatial computing, such as immersive video, 3D design, and games.

Typical uses include watching movies on a giant virtual screen, working with multiple floating windows, viewing and recording spatial photos and videos, and previewing 3D models. Mac Virtual Display mirrors a Mac into the headset, and enterprise users explore training, design review, and remote collaboration. Apple Intelligence features are being added to visionOS, including writing tools and a smarter Siri, and the device’s sensors power features like hand tracking and scene understanding.

item.title: AudioEye
item.description:
AudioEye is a web accessibility service. Its scanner tests pages against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, finding problems such as missing alt text, poor contrast, unlabeled form fields, and keyboard traps. A script added to the site can then apply fixes automatically for many of these issues, which is quicker than editing every page by hand.

Automation covers only part of the job, so AudioEye also offers expert audits, user testing with people who have disabilities, and managed services. It provides monitoring, reports, and accessibility statements, and integrates with common platforms like Shopify and WordPress. Companies use it to show a good faith effort toward compliance.

item.title: Azure AI Document Intelligence
item.description: Azure AI Document Intelligence reads documents so applications can use the data. Its layout model finds text, tables, headings, and selection marks, and prebuilt models recognize common document types such as invoices, receipts, business cards, identity documents, and many tax and mortgage forms, returning fields like totals, dates, and names with confidence scores. You can train custom models with a small number of examples to extract the fields in your own forms.

item.title: Ben's Bites
item.description:
Ben’s Bites began as a daily email in which Ben Tossell shared what he found interesting in AI. It became popular because he wrote like a person rather than a press release, picking tools worth trying and giving short reactions. Readers range from founders and developers to curious non-technical people who want to keep up.

Over time, it expanded beyond a single email. A community of subscribers shares tips and projects, and there are resources such as prompt collections and a list of tools. Some content is for paying members, while the main newsletter remains free. Sponsorships support the free edition and are labeled.

item.title: Google Cloud Text-to-Speech
item.description:
Google Cloud Text-to-Speech gives developers speech synthesis built on the technology behind Google’s assistants. A request with text returns audio in formats like MP3 or WAV, with a choice of voices and languages. The newer voice families, such as WaveNet and the Chirp generation, sound much more natural than traditional synthetic voices, and there are many accents and genders to choose from.

Developers can fine-tune delivery with SSML, adding pauses, emphasis, pronunciation, and speed. The service supports long audio synthesis for audiobooks and narration, and streaming for real-time applications such as voice assistants and interactive voice response systems. Customers can request a custom voice trained on their own recordings, with strict requirements, and the service integrates with other Google Cloud tools.

item.title: Headway
item.description:
Headway offers book summaries you can read or listen to in minutes. Each summary covers the main ideas of a nonfiction title, such as business, psychology, or self-improvement, so users can sample many books quickly. Audio versions suit commutes and workouts.

The app leans on habit building. Users set daily goals, track streaks, and get reminders, and collections organize summaries by theme and goal. Quizzes and flashcards help retain what was read, and AI features personalize recommendations.

item.title: HoneyBook
item.description:
HoneyBook is designed for people who sell services, such as photographers, designers, coaches, and consultants. A client inquiry arrives through a form, the owner sends a proposal with a contract and an invoice, and the client signs and pays online, all within a single flow. This replaces a patchwork of documents, email threads, and payment apps.

Other features support day-to-day work. Automations send reminders and follow-ups, a scheduler lets clients book meetings, and a client portal keeps messages, files, and payments in one timeline. Templates for proposals and questionnaires make repeat work faster, and AI helps draft emails and project descriptions. Reports show income and pipeline.

item.title: Merlin Bird ID
item.description:
Merlin makes bird identification easy for beginners and experts. You can answer a few questions about where and when you saw a bird, its size, colors, and behavior, and Merlin suggests species. Photo ID uses image recognition to name a bird from a picture, and Sound ID listens to birdsong through your phone’s microphone in real time and shows which species are singing, which many users find astonishing.

The app is built on data from eBird, a huge citizen science project where birdwatchers log sightings, and machine learning trained on millions of photos and recordings. Downloadable regional packs let you identify birds without cell service, which helps in the field. Each species has photos, sounds, maps, and information, and a life list lets you track birds you have seen.

item.title: Rasa
item.description:
Rasa is a toolkit for developers who build conversational assistants. It started with machine learning components for understanding user messages and managing dialogue, and has evolved to combine language models with structured business logic. Teams define flows for tasks such as updating an address or booking an appointment, and the model handles the language.

Control is its main appeal. Companies can host Rasa themselves, keeping conversations and customer data within their own environment, and decide exactly what the assistant is allowed to do. That suits banks, telecoms, and healthcare organizations with strict privacy and compliance needs, and it reduces the risk of a language model improvising.

item.title: Rask AI
item.description:
Rask AI makes video localization simpler. You upload a video or provide a link, and the tool transcribes the speech, translates it into one of many languages, and produces a new audio track with a synthetic voice. Editing tools let you correct the transcript and translation before generating the final version.

Additional features improve the result. Voice cloning keeps the speaker’s voice character in the new language, and lip sync adjusts the mouth movements to match the dubbed audio. It also handles multiple speakers, subtitles, and exports, and offers an API for teams that localize at scale.

item.title: SAP Concur
item.description:
Concur is a staple of corporate finance. Employees book travel, capture receipts with a phone, and submit expense reports, which flow through approvals and into accounting systems. Policies are applied automatically, flagging out-of-policy spending, and credit card feeds reduce manual entry. Finance teams use it to control costs, reimburse employees, and meet audit requirements.

The platform has grown to include invoice and travel management, with integrations to airlines, hotels, and payment providers. AI supports automatic receipt reading, categorization, audit of expenses to detect errors or fraud, and assistance through SAP’s Joule for answering questions and completing tasks. Reporting provides visibility into travel and spending trends.

item.title: Storytel
item.description:
Storytel gives readers and listeners unlimited access to a library through a monthly subscription. The company began in Sweden and is a major audiobook service across the Nordics, with strong local-language catalogs in many markets, including Spanish, Polish, and Indian languages. Listeners use the mobile app to stream or download books and can adjust speed and set sleep timers.

The service has experimented with AI. VoiceSwitcher lets a listener change between the original human narrator and a synthetic voice for the same book, which helps with books that would not otherwise be recorded. Storytel also uses AI voices to expand its catalog and to translate books, an approach that has drawn debate about the role of human narrators.

item.title: Superwhisper
item.description:
Superwhisper is a dictation tool. You press a shortcut, speak, and the text appears wherever your cursor is, in an email, a document, or a code editor. Because it can run speech recognition models on your own machine, nothing has to be sent to the cloud, which matters for privacy and works without an internet connection.

Modes make it more than plain transcription. A mode can clean up filler words, format the text as an email or meeting notes, translate it, or follow a custom prompt that uses a language model to rewrite what you said. It also understands context from the app you are in, and supports many languages and voice models, including cloud options for higher accuracy.

item.title: Synthesizer V
item.description:
Synthesizer V is a singing voice synthesizer. A musician enters notes in a piano roll, types lyrics under each note, and the software sings them in a chosen voice. Parameters control pitch, vibrato, breathiness, and timing, so a producer can shape the performance rather than accept a flat robotic output.

The AI voice databases are the main attraction. They are trained on real singers and sound more natural than older concatenative systems, and some support several languages with a single voice. Vocal modes change the style, such as a softer or more intense delivery. Synthesizer V runs as a standalone editor or as a plugin in digital audio workstations, and a free version offers limited features.

item.title: Synthflow
item.description:
Synthflow is a no-code voice agent platform. A user designs the call flow in a visual editor, picks a voice, connects a phone number, and the agent handles calls, such as answering questions, booking appointments, and qualifying leads. Integrations connect calendars and CRMs.

Agencies resell the platform with white-label options, building agents for dental offices, home services, and similar businesses. Analytics show call outcomes and transcripts.

Synthflow is paid, with plans by minutes. Voice agents need testing for accuracy and disclosure of AI use. Alternatives include Retell AI, Vapi, Bland AI, Air AI, and PolyAI. Synthflow suits agencies and small businesses deploying voice agents.

item.title: Talkspace
item.description:
Talkspace lets people get mental health care remotely. Users complete an assessment, are matched with a licensed therapist, and can communicate through messaging, live video, or audio sessions, which makes treatment convenient and sometimes more affordable than in-person visits. Psychiatry services provide evaluations and medication management where appropriate.

A major difference from some competitors is insurance coverage: many users can pay with commercial insurance or Medicare plans through Talkspace, and employers and health plans offer it as a benefit. The company has added AI tools for matching, documentation, and safety monitoring, and is exploring ways AI can support providers while keeping therapy human. It publishes research on outcomes.

item.title: Zencastr
item.description:
Zencastr was built for remote podcast interviews. Instead of recording a call, it captures each participant’s microphone on their own device and uploads the separate tracks, which produces cleaner audio than the compressed stream you hear during a call. Guests join through a link in their browser, with no account needed.

Beyond recording, it offers tools for finishing a show. Automatic post-production levels audio and removes silence, an editor allows basic cuts, and AI features generate transcripts, summaries, and show notes. Video recording and a hosting option cover more of the workflow, and exports go to editing programs.

item.title: Milan Voice AI
item.description:
Milan Voice AI generates speech for creators and developers. Users type text and choose or create a voice, with options to clone a voice from a short sample or describe a new one. Multi-speaker mode takes a script with several characters and produces a dialogue, useful for podcasts, audiobooks, and videos.

Typical uses include narration, character voices, and prototypes of voice features. An API supports integration into apps. Voice cloning requires permission from the person whose voice is copied, and synthetic audio should be disclosed where appropriate.

item.title: AppFolio
item.description:
AppFolio runs the daily operations of a property management business. Staff list vacancies on rental sites, screen applicants, sign leases, collect rent online, and track maintenance requests and vendors. Owners receive statements and reports, and residents use a portal and app to pay and submit requests.

AI features take over routine communication. An assistant answers common tenant questions by text at any hour, qualifies leads, schedules showings, and flags maintenance requests that need attention. Analytics help managers see trends in occupancy, delinquency, and costs, and accounting tools are designed for property trust accounting.

item.title: Hippocratic AI
item.description:
Hippocratic AI focuses on non-diagnostic work in healthcare. Its agents call patients to check on recovery after discharge, remind them to take medication, prepare them for procedures, and monitor chronic conditions. The calls are long, patient conversations that clinical staff rarely have time to make.

Safety is the stated priority. The company tests its models with clinicians and designs the agents to stay within defined roles, escalating to a nurse or doctor when a patient reports symptoms that need attention. Health systems deploy them to extend staff capacity and reach patients between visits.

item.title: Smartify
item.description:
Smartify is an app for cultural venues. A visitor opens it in a partner museum, scans an artwork with the camera, and the app identifies it and shows background, artist information, and audio commentary. Collections can be saved for later.

Museums use it to enrich visits without installing hardware, and to learn what visitors engage with. The platform includes tools for creating tours and for accessibility. Some partners are major institutions.

item.title: Spectora
item.description:
Spectora is software for home inspection businesses. Inspectors document a property on a phone or tablet, adding photos, notes, and ratings, and Spectora compiles a professional report that can be delivered to clients and agents. Scheduling, agreements, and payment tools run the business side.

AI speeds up the slow part. It helps summarize defects, produce clear language for findings, and organize repair requests, and voice dictation turns spoken notes into text. Reports include summaries that buyers and agents can use during negotiations.

item.title: Trinka
item.description:
Trinka is built for scholarly and professional documents. It reviews text for grammar, style, and consistency with academic conventions, and understands field-specific terms in areas like medicine, engineering, and law. Suggestions explain why a change is recommended.

Extra tools check for plagiarism and consistency, offer paraphrasing, and run publication readiness checks. Plugins work with Microsoft Word and browsers, and a web editor is available.

Trinka has a free tier and paid plans. Authors should follow journal policies on AI-assisted editing. Alternatives include Paperpal, Grammarly, Writefull, Wordvice AI, and QuillBot. Trinka suits researchers and students polishing manuscripts.

item.title: MagicShot
item.description:
MagicShot takes an all-in-one approach to generative media. Rather than paying for a different service for each task, users get a single workspace for generating images, creating video, building avatars, making product shots, and producing voiceovers, all drawing on one pool of credits.

That suits marketers and small businesses who need a bit of everything. Tools include background replacement, upscaling, style transfer, and templates for ads and social posts. Convenience comes with some compromise, as individual tools may be less advanced than specialized products.

item.title: MosMos
item.description:
MosMos is a dictation and meeting tool for Mac. A user speaks and text appears in the active app, formatted to fit the context: casual in a chat, structured in a document, code-friendly in an editor. A personal glossary learns names and technical terms, reducing repeated mistakes.

In meetings, MosMos can record and transcribe with labels for each speaker and produce notes and action items afterward. Combining dictation and meeting features in one app saves switching between tools.

item.title: Aloud
item.description:
Aloud addresses the gap between what a developer means and what ends up in a written bug report or feature request. It records voice, screen, and a live transcript while someone talks through an app the way they naturally would, pointing at elements and changing their mind mid-sentence. It then converts the recording into a clean set of instructions.

The output is formatted so coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex can act on it directly. The tool flags anything that could be read two ways and attaches relevant screenshots, which cuts down on back-and-forth. Speech transcription runs locally through Whisper, so recordings stay on the Mac and are not uploaded, which matters for work on client or proprietary code.

item.title: Careforce AI
item.description:
Careforce provides AI workers for healthcare administration. Agents place outbound calls and texts to patients, such as to schedule overdue screenings, confirm appointments, and collect information before a visit. They handle follow-up and rescheduling, which often falls through in busy offices.

The company says its agents support many languages and can work across scheduling systems and payer portals, which lets clinics reach patients who might otherwise be missed. Scripts are configurable for different campaigns, such as preventive care outreach and post-operative check-ins.

item.title: Encore AI
item.description:
Encore AI builds on conversation data. It analyzes recordings of calls and chats to learn which behaviors lead to good outcomes, such as how top reps handle objections or open a conversation. Those patterns become the basis for AI agents that talk with customers.

The agents can take calls or messages themselves or support human reps with live guidance. The idea is to scale the best performers’ approach across a team instead of relying on training alone. Companies with large volumes of calls and recorded history are the target.

item.title: OpenAI Presence
item.description:
Presence aims to let companies put OpenAI-powered agents on the front line of conversations. Businesses configure agents that talk with customers by phone or chat and handle employee requests, connecting them to company systems so they can look up information and take actions.

The platform combines the models with enterprise features: tools for building and testing agents, integrations, monitoring, and controls to keep agents within policy. It competes with specialized customer service AI vendors and with platforms from other model providers.

item.title: Qualcomm AI Hub
item.description:
Qualcomm AI Hub targets on-device AI for phones, PCs, and other products built with Qualcomm chips. A developer uploads a model, and the service converts and optimizes it for the target hardware, then runs it on real devices in the cloud to measure speed and accuracy.

A library of ready-to-run models, such as vision, speech, and language models, saves time. Profiling shows where a model spends time and memory, guiding further tuning. The goal is to make it easy to run AI locally, with benefits for privacy, cost, and latency.

item.title: Veo 2
item.description:
Veo 2 generated short high-resolution clips from text or image prompts. It stood out for understanding cinematic language, such as lens choices and camera moves, and for physics that looked plausible, with fewer odd distortions.

It was offered through Google’s creative tools and API before being succeeded by Veo 3, which added native audio and further improvements. Many users moved to the newer model for quality and sound.

Check Google’s documentation for the currently supported models. Alternatives include Veo 3, Runway, Kling, Luma, and Pika. Veo 2 is of interest mainly to people comparing generations of video models.

item.title: Veo 3
item.description:
Veo 3 produces short video clips from text or image prompts with sound included. Earlier video models were silent and required separate audio work; Veo 3 creates speech, effects, and music that match the action, which makes clips feel more complete.

It is available in Google’s Gemini app, in Flow, a filmmaking tool, and through APIs for developers. Filmmakers and marketers use it for concept videos, ads, and social content, and it is known for realistic physics and prompt following.

item.title: Whisper
item.description:
Whisper is a speech-to-text model trained on a very large and varied collection of multilingual audio. That training made it unusually robust: it copes with accents, background noise, and technical vocabulary better than many earlier systems, and it works across dozens of languages. It also detects the spoken language automatically, adds punctuation, and can translate speech from other languages into English text.

The model is released as open source with several sizes, from small ones that run on a laptop to large ones that need a good GPU. That openness led to a wide ecosystem: faster versions such as whisper.cpp and faster-whisper, tools that add timestamps and speaker labels, and many apps for transcription, subtitles, and dictation that use it behind the scenes. OpenAI also offers it through its API for people who do not want to host it.

item.title: Neets AI
item.description:
Neets AI offers speech synthesis through a simple API. Developers send text and choose a voice, and the service returns audio. It emphasizes variety of voices, speed, and low cost, which suits projects that generate large volumes of audio, such as reading articles aloud.

Typical users include app developers, content publishers, and teams building voice agents. Voice quality is good for many purposes, though the top-tier commercial providers may offer more emotion and control. Streaming support makes it usable for interactive applications.

item.title: Soundful
item.description:
Soundful helps creators find music without licensing hassles. A user picks a genre, mood, and tempo, and the platform generates a track that can be customized and downloaded. The pitch is that each track is unique and cleared for use in videos, streams, and podcasts.

It serves YouTubers, streamers, marketers, and podcasters who need background music at scale. Different plans set what usage rights apply, including for monetized content and for commercial work.

item.title: Supademo
item.description:
Supademo makes product demos quickly. A user records clicks through an app with a browser extension, and Supademo converts them into a step-by-step interactive demo with callouts, which can be edited, branded, and embedded on a site or emailed.

AI adds voiceover narration and translations, and helps write step text. Analytics show who viewed a demo and where they stopped. The tool is also used for onboarding guides and help documentation.

item.title: Transistor
item.description:
Transistor is designed for people who run more than one podcast. A single account can host unlimited shows, which suits agencies, companies, and networks, and plans are based on downloads and team size instead of per-show fees. Episodes distribute to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other apps through an RSS feed Transistor manages.

Other features address professional needs. Private podcasts let companies share internal or members-only audio, embeddable players and a branded website help promote shows, and detailed analytics show downloads and audience. Collaboration features give team members access to specific shows, and integrations connect with Zapier and other tools. AI tools support transcripts and episode copy.

item.title: Yellow.ai
item.description:
Yellow.ai builds AI agents for customer and employee service. A company connects it to systems such as CRMs and ticketing, trains it on content, and deploys across websites, messaging apps, and phone lines. The agents answer questions and complete tasks in many languages.

The platform emphasizes multilingual support, strong in markets such as India, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Tools for building, testing, and monitoring agents, along with analytics, support operations teams. Handoff to human agents is built in.

item.title: The Audio Stuff
item.description:
The Audio Stuff covers personal audio gear with an emphasis on independence. Reviews of headphones, in-ear monitors, speakers, digital-to-analog converters, and amplifiers combine listening impressions with objective measurements, and the site states that it does not publish sponsored reviews. Comparisons and buying guides help readers navigate crowded categories.

For people buying audio equipment, the combination of measured data and subjective notes is useful. Frequency response graphs and other measurements show how products behave, which helps predict how they will sound, and the writing explains what that means for different music and preferences. The site also covers news and recommendations for budgets.

item.title: Appen
item.description:
Appen is one of the long-standing companies behind AI training data. Machine learning models need large amounts of labeled examples, such as transcribed speech, tagged images, ranked answers, and annotated documents, and Appen supplies them through a global crowd of contributors plus managed teams. Its customers have included major technology companies, and its work has fed search, voice assistants, and recommendation systems.

The services now lean toward generative AI. Appen provides data for aligning large language models, such as human preference rankings, expert-written examples, and red-teaming to find unsafe behavior. It also offers multimodal and speech datasets, coding data, and model evaluation services that test how a system performs in many languages and regions. A platform manages the workflows, quality checks, and contributor payments.

item.title: Audible
item.description:
Audible made audiobooks mainstream. Members get monthly credits to buy audiobooks they keep, plus access to a catalog of included titles, podcasts, and originals, and they can listen through the app on phones, tablets, and smart speakers. Features such as variable speed, bookmarks, sleep timers, and syncing between listening and reading with Kindle books make it practical for commuting and chores.

Technology is changing how titles are made. Audible has been introducing AI narration for publishers and authors who cannot afford a human narrator, and AI-powered translation and dubbing for audiobooks, alongside AI-based recommendations and summaries. Human narrators remain central to the premium experience, and the shift has prompted debate among narrators and listeners about quality and the future of the profession.

item.title: Augury
item.description:
Augury helps factories and facilities avoid unexpected equipment failures. Small wireless sensors attach to machines such as motors, pumps, fans, and compressors and measure vibration, temperature, and other signals. The data goes to the cloud, where machine learning models trained on large numbers of machines identify patterns that signal a developing problem, such as bearing wear or misalignment, often weeks before a breakdown.

The platform sends alerts with a diagnosis and recommended action, so maintenance teams can plan repairs during scheduled downtime instead of reacting to a failure. Dashboards show the health of assets across plants, and the service has expanded to include process monitoring and insights into production performance. Industries include food and beverage, chemicals, pulp and paper, and building management.

item.title: Blinkist
item.description:
Blinkist is designed for people who want the main ideas of a book without reading all of it. Editors and writers distill nonfiction titles in business, psychology, science, health, and self-improvement into short summaries, with key takeaways and often a quick audio version. Users listen on a commute or skim on a break, and it’s used as a way to preview a book before deciding to read it fully.

The app has broadened with audiobooks, original content, and tools such as highlighting and collections of titles by topic. AI features include personalized recommendations and generated summaries or answers based on its library, and an AI assistant that lets users ask questions about topics. Audio can be downloaded for offline listening.

item.title: Clarifai
item.description: Clarifai started as an image recognition API and has grown into a broader AI platform. Teams use it to find and call models for vision, language, and audio tasks, to train their own models on labeled data, and to run them in production. It includes tools for organizing and labeling data, searching images and video, and building workflows that chain several models together. Industries such as retail, media, and public sector have used it to classify content and find objects in large collections.

item.title: Deepdub
item.description: Deepdub works with studios, streamers, and media companies that need content in many languages. Its technology translates the dialogue and generates new speech in the target language, in a voice that matches the original performer, with timing that fits the picture. The goal is dubbing that carries over emotion and character, not the flat voice of a basic text-to-speech engine. It supports over a hundred languages and uses licensed voices, which matters for rights and union considerations.

item.title: Dubverse
item.description:
Dubverse helps creators reach audiences who speak other languages. You upload a video or paste a link, and the platform transcribes the speech, translates the script, and generates a dubbed voice track in the target language, timed to match the original. It supports a range of languages, including many Indian ones, and lets you edit the transcript and translation before the voice is produced, which matters for accuracy.

Features support a full localization workflow. You can choose among voices, adjust speed, and edit individual lines, and the platform can add subtitles. An API supports automation for companies that process a lot of content, and a text-to-speech studio produces voiceovers for videos without translation. Typical customers are YouTubers, e-learning teams, news and entertainment publishers, and brands that run content in several markets.

item.title: Hinge
item.description:
Hinge takes a different approach from swipe-first dating apps. Profiles are built from photos plus written or voice answers to prompts, which give people something specific to respond to. Users like or comment on a particular part of a profile, which starts a conversation with context.

The app uses algorithms to suggest people likely to be compatible, based on preferences and behavior, and has added AI tools such as prompt feedback to help people write better profiles. It limits how many likes a user can send, which encourages more selective choices, and offers premium tiers.

item.title: Lexalytics
item.description: Lexalytics builds natural language processing for businesses that need to make sense of large amounts of text. Its Salience engine reads reviews, survey comments, support tickets, social posts, and call transcripts and returns structured information: whether the sentiment is positive or negative, which products or people are mentioned, what themes recur, and what the author intends. Analysts can then count, trend, and compare these signals instead of reading comments one by one.

item.title: MyFitnessPal
item.description:
MyFitnessPal is the best-known food diary app. You log what you eat by searching a database of packaged foods, restaurant meals, and homemade recipes, and the app totals calories and macronutrients against daily goals. It syncs with fitness trackers and apps, so exercise adjusts your targets, and it records weight and measurements over time. Millions of people use it for weight loss, muscle gain, or general awareness.

Its size is its strength. The food database is huge, though many entries are user-submitted and can contain errors, so it pays to choose verified items. Features include barcode scanning, recipe import, meal scanning with AI to log from a photo, and voice logging. Premium adds more detailed nutrient tracking, custom goals, macro presets, and meal planning, while a free version covers basic logging.

item.title: NaturalReader
item.description:
NaturalReader turns reading into listening. You paste text, upload a document or PDF, or use the Chrome extension to read a web page, and it reads aloud in a voice you choose, with adjustable speed. Highlighting of each word as it is spoken helps learners follow along, and the tool supports many languages and accents. OCR features can read text from images and scanned pages.

It serves education and accessibility needs. Students with dyslexia, ADHD, or visual impairments use it to access materials, professionals use it to review documents on the go, and teachers use it with classroom content. Premium plans offer higher-quality AI voices, more file formats, and commercial use for creating audio, while a free version covers personal use with basic voices.

item.title: Papercup
item.description:
Papercup offered dubbing for media companies. Its system translated the dialogue of a video and generated speech in another language that matched the tone and timing of the original, with human translators and editors checking the results. Publishers, broadcasters, and content owners used it to put news, documentaries, and entertainment in front of audiences in new markets without paying for traditional dubbing studios.

The approach mixed machine speed with human oversight. Linguists reviewed translations, adjusted phrasing, and corrected pronunciation, which kept quality higher than fully automatic dubbing and made the service suitable for professional content. It also let customers keep control over the voice style and brand.

item.title: Adobe Enhance Speech
item.description: Enhance Speech is a simple tool with a dramatic effect. You upload a recording of a voice, such as an interview, podcast, voiceover, or video narration, and the AI processes it to remove noise, reverb, and room echo, and rebalances the voice. In moments, a recording made on a phone in a kitchen can sound much closer to something recorded in a studio. It has become popular among creators who record in imperfect spaces.

item.title: Adobe Podcast
item.description:
Adobe Podcast started with one very useful trick: you upload a voice recording made in a noisy room, and it comes back sounding like it was recorded in a studio. Enhance Speech removes hiss, echo, and background noise and evens out the voice. People use it to rescue interview audio, remote recordings, and phone-quality clips, and it works well on single speakers talking clearly.

The wider product is a browser-based recording and editing studio. You can record yourself or a remote guest, then edit by deleting words in the transcript, much like editing a text document. Features that clean up speech, adjust volume, and add music or sound effects sit alongside it. A mic check tool tests how your setup sounds before you start. Because everything runs in the browser, there is nothing to install, and files can be exported for use in other editors.

item.title: Adobe Premiere Pro AI
item.description: Premiere Pro is a timeline-based video editor used for everything from YouTube videos and corporate content to broadcast and feature work. It handles most camera formats, supports proxy workflows for heavy footage, and connects directly to After Effects, Audition, and other Adobe apps. That connection is a large part of why editing teams keep using it: a project can pass between an editor, a colorist, and a motion designer without leaving the Adobe ecosystem.

item.title: AIVA
item.description: AIVA, short for Artificial Intelligence Virtual Artist, was built to compose music, with an early emphasis on classical and cinematic styles. You pick a style from a library of hundreds, set the length and key, and it generates a track. You can also upload an audio or MIDI file as an influence, or define your own chord progression. Video creators, game developers, podcasters, and advertisers use it to get background music without hiring a composer.

item.title: Altered AI
item.description:
Altered focuses on voice conversion, sometimes called speech-to-speech. You record a performance, and the system re-voices it in another voice from its library while keeping the timing, emotion, and delivery of the original. That differs from text-to-speech, where the machine invents the performance. For productions, it means one actor can voice several characters, or a performance can be changed to match a different character without a second recording session.

The tools are designed for professionals. Altered Studio provides a way to process recordings and fine-tune results, and the platform includes text-to-speech and voice cloning options for productions that need them. Typical customers are game studios, audiobook makers, animation and film teams, and agencies that localize content. Licensed voices matter in this field, since using someone’s voice without permission raises legal and ethical issues.

item.title: Animaker
item.description:
Animaker lets people without animation skills make animated videos. You choose a template or start from scratch, add characters, props, backgrounds, and text, and arrange them on a timeline. A character builder customizes avatars with facial expressions and actions, and ready-made assets cover business, education, and storytelling scenes. It also supports whiteboard-style videos, infographic videos, and live-action editing, with exports up to 4K.

AI tools shorten the production steps. Text-to-animation turns a script into a rough animated scene, voiceover tools generate narration in many voices and languages, and translation and auto-subtitle features help localize videos. Teams use it for training videos, product explainers, school lessons, social media clips, and internal communications, where hiring an animation studio would be too costly.

item.title: Auphonic
item.description:
Auphonic automates the finishing steps of audio production. You upload a recording, such as a podcast episode or interview, and it applies adaptive leveling to even out volume differences between speakers, normalizes loudness to the standards used by streaming and broadcast, reduces background noise and hum, and applies filtering to improve clarity. The result is consistent, professional sounding audio with little manual work.

It supports multitrack recordings, where each person is recorded separately, and balances them automatically. Additional features include speech recognition to create transcripts, chapter marks, and exports to podcast hosts and cloud storage, and an API allows batch processing. Presets and a web interface make it approachable for non-engineers, and it’s used by independent podcasters, radio stations, and educators.

item.title: BILL AI
item.description:
BILL helps businesses handle bills and payments without paper and manual entry. Vendors’ invoices arrive by email or upload, the system extracts the details, routes them for approval, and schedules payment by ACH, check, or card. On the receivables side, it sends invoices to customers and collects payments.

AI takes on the data entry. It reads invoice fields, suggests accounting categories, matches invoices to purchase orders and receipts, and flags duplicates or unusual items. Integrations with QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite, and other accounting systems keep the books in sync, and spend management tools add corporate cards and expense tracking.

item.title: Buzzsprout
item.description:
Buzzsprout focuses on being the easiest way to get a podcast online. You upload an audio file, add show notes, and publish, and it distributes the episode to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other directories through an RSS feed it manages. It provides an embeddable player for your website, detailed download statistics, and tools for promoting episodes on social media.

Additional features help creators improve and grow. Magic Mastering automatically cleans up and balances audio loudness, an AI transcription service creates transcripts, and tools can generate chapters, episode titles, and descriptions. Dynamic content features and a way to import an existing podcast make switching easy. Monetization options include support from listeners and ads in some plans.

item.title: Cartesia
item.description:
Cartesia focuses on speed in voice AI. Its Sonic models, built on state-space model architectures instead of only transformers, generate natural-sounding speech with very low latency, so a voice agent can start speaking almost as soon as a response is ready. That matters for phone calls and live assistants, where delays feel awkward. The company also offers voice cloning and control over emotion and speaking rate.

The platform has grown into a set of real-time voice building blocks. Sonic handles text-to-speech, Ink handles speech-to-text, and tools for managed voice agents help companies deploy agents that answer phone calls. Developers connect through APIs and SDKs, and Cartesia works with common voice agent frameworks and telephony providers. Multilingual support lets one system serve customers in different languages.

item.title: Casetext
item.description: Casetext began as a community site where lawyers annotated and shared case law, then grew into a legal research service with tools such as a brief-checking feature called Parallel Search, which found relevant cases using natural language. It was among the first legal technology companies to build on large language models, and its CoCounsel assistant could review documents, summarize depositions, draft research memos, and help prepare contract analyses with citations to sources.

item.title: Cleanfeed
item.description:
Cleanfeed lets people record or broadcast audio over the internet without installing software. A host creates a session, guests join by link in a browser, and the platform streams audio with low delay and records each participant on a separate track. It is popular with radio and podcast teams who need dependable quality.

The audio chain is a focus. It offers a noise gate, level controls, and processing options that tidy up voices, plus connections for studio equipment and phone callers. Producers can monitor and route audio, record backups, and download multitrack files. A newer version improves collaboration and integration with video.

item.title: Cleanvoice
item.description: Cleanvoice does one job: it cleans up speech. You upload a podcast episode, interview, or video, and it finds the places where a speaker said “um” or “uh,” paused for too long, made lip smacks or breath sounds, or repeated a word. It removes them and returns a tidier file. Editing these by hand takes a long time, and a one-hour recording can contain hundreds of them, so automating it saves real hours for podcasters and video creators.

item.title: D-ID
item.description:
D-ID became known for animating still photos. You upload a portrait and add a script or audio, and the platform produces a video in which the person appears to speak, with lip movement and facial expressions. That idea grew into a full avatar platform: a studio where you create presenters, choose voices and languages, and generate videos for training, marketing, and customer communication.

Beyond videos, D-ID provides tools for interactive use. An API lets developers generate talking avatars in their own applications, and real-time agents combine an avatar, a language model, and a voice so that a digital person can hold a conversation on a website or kiosk. The company also works on privacy technology, with its origins in tools that protect faces from recognition systems.

item.title: DeepL
item.description:
DeepL built its reputation on translations that read more naturally than many competitors, especially for European languages. You paste text or upload a document, such as a Word file, PDF, or PowerPoint, and get a translation that keeps the formatting. Options let you choose formal or informal tone, add glossaries for specific terms, and see alternative wordings for phrases.

The product has expanded into a broader language platform. DeepL Write improves and rephrases text in the same language, DeepL Voice translates live conversations and meetings, and browser extensions and desktop apps translate as you work. An API serves developers and enterprises, and newer agent features automate tasks. Business plans add data security, which promises that texts are not used for training, plus team glossaries.

item.title: Descript
item.description:
Descript changed podcast editing by turning audio into text. After you record or import an episode, it transcribes it, and you cut, move, and delete sections by editing the words, which is much faster than working on waveforms. Filler words and long pauses can be removed in bulk, and multitrack editing, music, and effects are available for more polished shows.

Recording and polishing tools are built in. Remote recording captures guests in high quality, Studio Sound improves voice clarity and reduces noise, and an Overdub feature can fix mistakes with a synthetic version of your voice. AI assistants draft titles, descriptions, and show notes, suggest chapters, and generate clips and audiograms for social media. Episodes can be published to hosting platforms or exported.

item.title: Descript
item.description:
Descript changed how many people edit podcasts and videos. After recording, Descript transcribes the audio, and deleting a word from the transcript cuts it from the media. That makes editing feel like working in a document, which is friendlier for people without video editing experience.

AI tools extend the idea. Studio Sound improves audio quality in one click, filler word removal cleans speech, eye contact correction adjusts gaze, and the underlord assistant performs edits from instructions. Voice cloning lets you fix a word by typing it, and text can drive screen recording, multi-track editing, and clips for social media.

item.title: Descript
item.description: Descript changed how many people edit audio and video. You upload a recording, it produces a transcript, and you cut, rearrange, and delete the media by editing the text like a document. Removing a sentence in the transcript removes it from the recording. For podcasts, interviews, tutorials, and talking-head videos, that is much faster than working on a waveform, and people who have never used an editor can pick it up quickly.

item.title: Descript Studio Sound
item.description:
Studio Sound targets the common problem of recording in imperfect spaces. Apply it to a clip in Descript, and the AI removes noise, reduces echo and reverb, and evens out the voice, making recordings made on a laptop or phone sound much more professional. It works on a whole project or a selected portion and has an intensity setting, so you can balance cleanup against natural sound.

It is built into Descript’s editing workflow, so you can clean audio while editing the transcript, and it works on both audio and video projects. Podcasters, interviewers, educators, and video creators use it to rescue recordings from noisy environments. It can be combined with other features in Descript, such as filler word removal and eye contact correction for video.

item.title: Dolby.io
item.description:
Dolby.io brings Dolby’s audio expertise to developers as web services. A developer sends an audio or video file and receives a processed version: cleaner speech, reduced background noise, balanced loudness, or improved dialogue. These APIs fit podcast tools, video platforms, and conferencing products.

Other parts of the platform focus on real-time streaming. Millicast delivers low-latency video to large audiences, which suits live events, interactive broadcasts, and remote production. Analysis and transcoding APIs help prepare content for different devices.

item.title: ElevenLabs
item.description:
ElevenLabs is known for natural-sounding synthetic speech. Users type text and choose a voice, or clone a voice from a sample, and get audio that carries intonation and emotion. The platform supports dozens of languages and accents and offers a library of voices.

Its products now span several uses. Dubbing translates video into other languages while keeping the speaker’s voice, audiobook and narration tools produce long-form audio, and a conversational agent platform builds voice assistants that talk with customers in real time. Music and sound effect generation, plus speech to text, round out the suite. An API lets developers embed these features.

item.title: ElevenLabs
item.description: ElevenLabs is best known for text-to-speech that sounds like a person rather than a robot. You paste in a script, choose a voice from a large library or make your own, and the tool reads it with natural pacing and emotion. The same voice can speak dozens of languages, which makes it a popular option for audiobooks, YouTube narration, e-learning, game characters, and accessibility. Voice cloning builds a copy of a voice from a recording, and there are safeguards around it: you are meant to have the speaker’s permission, and some features require identity checks.

item.title: ElevenLabs Sound Effects
item.description:
ElevenLabs Sound Effects creates audio from a sentence. You describe the sound you need, such as a door creaking in an empty house or a crowd cheering in a stadium, and the model generates several options in seconds, which you can adjust for length and download. This helps video editors, game developers, podcasters, and filmmakers who otherwise search libraries for the right clip or record effects themselves.

The company also offers a Voice Isolator that separates speech from background noise and music, helping clean up interviews and field recordings. These tools fit alongside ElevenLabs’ text-to-speech, dubbing, and music features, so a creator can produce a full soundtrack in one place. An API allows developers to generate effects inside apps and games.

item.title: Flick AI
item.description:
Flick targets people who manage social media without a large team. It combines content planning with AI writing: you can brainstorm ideas, generate captions and post drafts in your own style, and organize them on a calendar before scheduling. A hashtag tool suggests relevant tags, and an analytics view helps you see what performs well.

An AI assistant trained on your past content tries to match your tone and topics, so drafts need less editing than generic output. The platform supports multiple networks, including Instagram, LinkedIn, and TikTok, and offers collaboration features for agencies or small teams to review and approve content. Prompts and templates help with common formats such as carousels and short videos.

item.title: Fliki
item.description:
Fliki turns written content into video. A user pastes a script, links an article, or writes a prompt, and the tool splits it into scenes, picks visuals from a stock library or generated media, and adds narration with a synthetic voice. The editor allows swapping clips, adjusting text, and changing voices.

A big draw is the range of voices and languages, which lets creators produce the same video in several markets. Avatars and voice cloning are available, and text to speech is offered as a standalone product for narration and audio. Marketers, educators, and YouTubers use it to repurpose content.

item.title: Google Assistant
item.description: Google Assistant is the voice assistant that ships on Android phones, Nest speakers and displays, Android Auto, Wear OS watches, and many third-party smart home devices. You wake it with a phrase or a button, then ask it to set a timer, add a calendar event, send a message, play music, or turn off the lights. It works well for short, concrete commands, and a large ecosystem of smart home brands supports it, which made it one of the more capable options for controlling a connected home.

item.title: Happy Scribe
item.description:
Happy Scribe converts speech into text. You upload an audio or video file, or connect a source like Zoom or YouTube, and receive a transcript in minutes with speaker labels and timestamps. It supports many languages and dialects, which suits journalists, researchers, podcasters, and companies that work in several markets. A browser editor lets you listen while you correct the text.

Subtitling is a major use. The service can generate subtitles and captions for videos, translate them into other languages, and export in standard formats for YouTube, Vimeo, and video editors. For cases where accuracy matters more, such as legal or broadcast work, you can order human-made transcripts and subtitles, which cost more and take longer. An API and integrations connect it to workflows.

item.title: HeyGen
item.description: HeyGen lets you make a talking-head video without filming. You choose an avatar or create your own from a short recording, paste or write a script, and HeyGen generates a video with natural speech and lip movement. It supports dozens of languages, and one of its popular uses is video translation: upload a video of yourself, and it produces a version in another language with your voice and matching lip movements. Marketers, trainers, and sales teams use it to produce content quickly.

item.title: Hume AI
item.description: Hume AI started from research on human emotion. Its models analyze the way people speak and show emotion, including tone, pace, and inflection, and its Empathic Voice Interface (EVI) uses that understanding in a conversational voice assistant. EVI listens to the user’s voice, picks up on cues like frustration or excitement, and adjusts its responses and speaking style accordingly, so a voice agent can feel more natural than one that only transcribes words.

item.title: Hypotenuse AI
item.description:
Hypotenuse AI is built for online stores with large catalogs. You upload a spreadsheet of products with attributes, and it writes descriptions for each one, in a consistent tone and optimized for search, saving the effort of writing hundreds or thousands of descriptions by hand. It can also produce category pages, meta descriptions, blog posts, and ad copy.

Features support brand and workflow. A brand voice setting keeps text aligned with a company’s style, a plagiarism check helps ensure uniqueness, and integrations connect with Shopify and other platforms to publish content directly. The product also offers AI image tools for creating and editing product images and backgrounds, which makes it a toolkit for content across a catalog.

item.title: InVideo
item.description:
InVideo targets creators and marketers who need many videos fast. In InVideo AI, you describe the video you want, such as a product explainer, a faceless YouTube video, or a social ad, and it writes a script, selects stock clips, adds a voiceover and music, and assembles it. You can then give plain-language instructions to change scenes, tone, or length, which makes iteration quick for people without editing skills.

The traditional editor remains for more control. It provides templates, a timeline, text and effects, and a large stock library, and it can turn blog posts and scripts into videos. Voice features include text-to-speech in many languages and voice cloning, and recent versions have added AI-generated video clips and avatars alongside stock footage. Exports are available in formats for different social platforms.

item.title: iZotope RX
item.description:
RX is the tool engineers reach for when audio is flawed. Its spectral display shows sound as an image, making it possible to see and remove specific problems, such as a cough, a phone buzz, or a chair squeak, without affecting the rest. Modules cover denoising, de-clicking, de-hum, de-reverb, de-clipping, and other repair tasks, and are used by post-production teams, podcast producers, forensic analysts, and musicians.

Machine learning powers its newer tools. Dialogue Isolate separates speech from background sounds, Music Rebalance lets you adjust the levels of vocals, bass, and drums in a finished mix, and Spectral Recovery restores high frequencies lost in low-quality files. Dialogue Contour and other features help produce consistent speech. It works as a standalone editor and as plugins in digital audio workstations and video editors.

item.title: Jasper
item.description:
For copywriting, Jasper offers more structure than a general chatbot. Marketers choose a format such as a Facebook ad, a product description, a landing page section, or an email sequence, supply the details, and get multiple options in their brand’s voice. The Brand Voice feature learns tone and style from examples, and a company knowledge base provides facts about products and audiences so the copy uses accurate claims.

Collaboration features suit teams. Shared templates and style guides keep writers consistent, and campaigns can be planned in one place with copy, images, and variations for different channels. An editor helps refine text, change tone, and check for plagiarism. Newer agent features help automate common marketing tasks, such as producing a set of assets from a brief.

item.title: Jasper
item.description:
As a marketing platform, Jasper aims to speed up the full path from a brief to a finished campaign. Marketers define their brand voice, audience, and product information once, then generate blog posts, social posts, ads, emails, and landing pages that follow those guidelines. Campaign tools help plan content around a launch, adapt messages for each channel, and keep versions organized.

The latest versions emphasize agents and workflows. Specialized agents handle tasks such as researching a topic, creating a content calendar, repurposing a webinar into several assets, and optimizing copy for search. Integrations connect with tools such as Google Docs, Webflow, and HubSpot, and analytics features tie content to performance. Controls let enterprises govern who can use what and ensure compliance with brand rules.

item.title: Jasper
item.description: Jasper was one of the first dedicated AI writing products and has focused on marketing teams that need a lot of on-brand content. You describe what you need, such as a product launch email or a set of ad variations, and it drafts the copy using your guidelines. Brand Voice learns your tone from sample content, and a knowledge base stores product details, audiences, and approved messaging, so output needs fewer corrections.

item.title: Krisp
item.description: Krisp installs as a virtual microphone and speaker, so it sits between your hardware and whatever calling app you use. It removes noise before it reaches the other person: barking dogs, keyboard clatter, traffic, and other voices in the room. It can also clean incoming audio, so a participant on a bad connection or in a loud space sounds clearer to you. Because it works with Zoom, Teams, Meet, Slack, and nearly any other app, one setup covers all of them.

item.title: Loudly
item.description:
Loudly offers music for people who need soundtracks without composing. Users can create tracks by choosing a genre, mood, and tempo, or by describing what they want in a prompt, and then download the result. A library of ready-made AI tracks lets you browse by genre and use case. It is intended for video creators, podcasters, streamers, game developers, and businesses that need background music.

Several features support practical use. A personalization option adjusts elements like instruments and structure, stems can be downloaded for editing, and an API allows developers to embed music generation in their own products, such as apps that need adaptive soundtracks. The company positions its music as safe for commercial use, with licenses that cover content on social platforms.

item.title: Lovo AI
item.description:
Lovo makes synthetic speech for creators and businesses. Users type or paste a script, choose a voice, and adjust tone, speed, and emphasis to generate narration. Genny, the editor, lets them place speech alongside video, images, and music in one timeline.

Voice cloning and a marketplace of voices expand the options, and the platform supports many languages. Typical uses are explainer videos, e-learning, ads, and audiobooks. An API provides access for developers.

item.title: MarketMan
item.description:
MarketMan is back-of-house software for food service. Operators record what they buy and use, build recipes with ingredient costs, and see the cost of each dish. When prices change or usage varies, the system flags it, helping managers protect margins.

Ordering and invoicing are handled in one place. Staff place orders with suppliers, receive deliveries, and match invoices to what arrived, which catches errors and short shipments. Forecasting tools predict how much to order based on sales history, and integrations connect with point of sale and accounting systems.

item.title: Murf
item.description: Murf is known for its studio, but its voice features are a separate reason people use it. The voice changer converts a recording of your own speech into a different voice from the library, keeping your timing and emotion, which suits people who want a polished sound without hiring talent. Voice cloning can create a custom voice for a brand or presenter, typically with consent and verification, and is offered mainly for business customers.

item.title: Murf
item.description:
Murf is aimed at people who need a professional voiceover without hiring a voice actor or booking a studio. In its browser-based studio, you paste a script, choose a voice, and adjust pitch, speed, and emphasis. Voices come in many accents and languages and suit narration, e-learning, product videos, ads, and presentations. You can add background music, line the audio up with video or slides, and export the result.

The platform has expanded to related audio jobs. Dubbing translates a video or audio file into other languages and keeps it timed to the original. An API gives developers text-to-speech for their own apps, including fast, streaming voices for conversational use. Murf Agents power voice calls and chat for customer service and similar needs, and a voice changer converts one voice into another. Team workspaces help companies share projects and keep audio consistent.

item.title: Notta
item.description: Notta turns speech into text for people who sit through many conversations. You can record in the mobile or web app, upload audio and video files, or let its assistant join Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams calls. The transcript appears in the app with speaker labels and timestamps, and you can search it, edit it, and share it. It supports a large number of languages, which suits international teams, journalists, and researchers.

item.title: OpenAI Realtime API
item.description:
The Realtime API changes how voice applications are built. Older systems chained speech recognition, a language model, and speech synthesis, adding delay at each step. The Realtime API handles audio in and audio out directly in one model, so responses start sooner and can include tone, pauses, and interruptions that sound natural.

Developers connect over WebRTC or WebSockets to stream audio and receive speech, text, and tool calls. It supports function calling, so a voice agent can look up data or take actions, and it can be used for phone agents, in-app assistants, and language practice.

item.title: Phrase
item.description:
Phrase helps companies translate software and content into many languages. Developers connect repositories and design tools, and new text is sent to translators or machine translation, then returned to the product when approved. Translation memory reuses earlier work and glossaries keep terminology consistent.

The platform brings together several products that grew from a merger: a translation management system, a string management tool for software teams, and a computer-assisted translation editor. AI translation engines and quality estimation reduce the amount of human review needed for lower-risk content.

item.title: Pictory
item.description:
Pictory is aimed at marketers and content creators who want video without editing skills. You paste a script or a blog URL, and the AI splits the text into scenes, picks stock clips and images for each, adds captions and music, and generates a voiceover. You can then edit scenes, swap visuals, and adjust the text with a simple storyboard-style editor.

Other features extend the same idea. Pictory can summarize a long video, such as a webinar or Zoom recording, into a short highlight reel, create captions, and generate text-to-video clips. A brand kit keeps colors and logos consistent, and integrations let teams pull content from articles. Typical uses are social media videos, explainers, and repurposing blog posts for video platforms.

item.title: Rev
item.description:
Rev started as a human transcription marketplace and added automatic transcription as speech recognition improved. Users upload audio or video, and receive a transcript within minutes from the AI service, or within hours from human transcribers who deliver higher accuracy. The choice lets you trade cost and speed for precision, which matters for legal proceedings, journalism, and broadcast captions.

Beyond transcripts, Rev offers captions and subtitles in many languages, translation, and a web editor for correcting and exporting text. Meeting tools record calls and produce notes, and an API supports developers who want to add transcription to products. Accessibility compliance is a big use, because captions help meet legal requirements for education and media.

item.title: Riverside
item.description: Riverside solves a familiar remote-recording problem: video calls compress audio and video, so the recording sounds and looks poor. Riverside records each person’s microphone and camera on their own device and uploads the files in the background. The result is uncompressed audio and up to 4K video, with each participant on a separate track, unaffected by a weak internet connection during the call. Hosts and guests join through a browser link without installing anything.

item.title: Sonix
item.description:
Sonix focuses on fast, accurate machine transcription with a polished editor. You upload a file or connect a source, and get a transcript with timestamps and speaker labels, which you can edit while listening and the text highlights as the audio plays. It supports over forty languages and can translate transcripts into many more. Journalists, researchers, podcasters, and video producers use it to turn recordings into searchable text.

Additional tools support publishing. Sonix exports subtitles and captions in standard formats, offers a media player that embeds the transcript, and provides search across all your files. Integrations and an API connect it with video editors like Premiere Pro and Final Cut, and Zoom. Teams can share folders and custom vocabulary to improve accuracy on specialized terms.

item.title: Speechify
item.description: Speechify turns reading into listening. You import text from the web, a PDF, an email, or a photo of a page, and the app reads it aloud at the speed you choose, highlighting the words as it goes. That makes it useful for catching up on articles while commuting, for studying, and for people with dyslexia or other reading differences, who often find audio easier to process. Apps for iOS, Android, Chrome, and the web sync your library.

item.title: Stability AI
item.description:
Stability AI helped start the open-source image generation boom with Stable Diffusion, a model anyone could download, run, and modify. The release spurred a huge community of tools, fine-tunes, and applications, and changed expectations about access to generative models.

The company has since released a family of models, including newer image generators, Stable Video Diffusion, Stable Audio for music and sound, and 3D tools. It sells API access and commercial licenses, and partners with enterprises, and with media and entertainment companies.

item.title: Stampli
item.description:
Stampli keeps the conversation about an invoice attached to the invoice. When a bill arrives, teams discuss it in context, approvers sign off, and the payment goes out, with no hunting through email threads. It connects to accounting systems and does not require replacing them.

Billy the Bot reads invoices, suggests coding and approvals based on past behavior, and flags anomalies. Payment tools handle payments and cards, and the platform provides audit trails and reporting.

item.title: Steve AI
item.description:
Steve AI is a text-to-video tool aimed at people who need videos without filming. You paste a script, an article, or a prompt, and the platform creates a video with scenes, characters or stock footage, text, voiceover, and music, which you can edit. It offers animated styles and live-action style videos built from stock clips.

It supports many typical use cases. Marketers create explainers and promos, educators make lesson videos, and social media managers turn blog posts into short clips. Options include different aspect ratios, branding, and a library of characters and backgrounds. Voiceover and avatar features add narration in various languages.

item.title: Suki AI
item.description:
Suki reduces the paperwork burden on doctors. With patient consent, its ambient system listens to the visit, converts the conversation into a structured clinical note in the specialty’s format, and places it in the electronic health record for review. Clinicians can also dictate or use voice commands to look up information, queue orders, and complete tasks hands-free.

The assistant extends beyond notes. It suggests billing codes based on the documentation, helps with information retrieval from the chart, and supports different specialties with tailored templates. Integration with major record systems is a priority, since adoption depends on fitting into existing workflows. Healthcare organizations use it to reduce time spent on documentation and clinician burnout.

item.title: Vapi
item.description:
Vapi handles the hard parts of voice agents. Developers define an assistant with a prompt and tools, connect a phone number, and Vapi orchestrates speech-to-text, the language model, and text-to-speech, with handling for interruptions and turn-taking. Bring-your-own provider choices allow swapping components.

Use cases include customer support lines, appointment scheduling, outbound calls, and voice assistants in apps. The platform includes testing, analytics, and call transfer features.

Vapi is billed by minutes plus provider costs. Voice calls are regulated, and callers should know they are speaking with an AI. Alternatives include Retell AI, Bland AI, Synthflow, Twilio ConversationRelay, and LiveKit. Vapi suits developers building voice agents.

item.title: WellSaid Labs
item.description:
WellSaid focuses on voiceovers for businesses. In its web studio, you type or paste a script, pick a voice, and generate narration with control over pacing, pronunciation, and emphasis. The voices are built from recordings by professional voice actors who agreed to the use, which gives companies a clear license position. Typical projects include training courses, explainer videos, product tours, corporate announcements, and audio for apps.

For larger teams, collaboration and control matter. Projects can be shared, commented on, and reviewed, and custom pronunciation settings keep brand names and technical terms consistent across a library of content. An API lets developers add speech to their own products, and integrations connect WellSaid to e-learning and creative tools. Enterprise plans emphasize security, privacy, and compliance, and custom voices can be created for a brand.

item.title: Zendesk
item.description:
Zendesk is one of the most widely used help desk systems. Customer messages from email, web chat, phone, WhatsApp, and social media become tickets in a shared workspace, where they can be routed, prioritized, and tracked against service targets. A help center and community forum let customers find answers themselves, and reports show response times and satisfaction. It scales from small support teams to large contact centers.

The current product is built around AI. AI agents take on requests from start to finish, answering from help articles and past conversations, and taking actions in connected systems when allowed. A copilot assists human agents by suggesting replies, summarizing long threads, and flagging urgent or unhappy customers. The platform has added contact center, workforce management, and quality assurance tools, and an employee service product that applies the same ideas to internal IT and HR requests.

item.title: ABBYY
item.description:
ABBYY has worked with optical character recognition for decades. Its FineReader software converts scanned pages and PDFs into editable text, and its enterprise products read invoices, contracts, IDs, and forms at scale. Machine learning classifies the type of document, locates key fields such as invoice totals and dates, and extracts the data in a structured form that other systems can use.

The platform has expanded into intelligent document processing. Pre-trained skills handle common document types without training, while companies can build custom models for their own forms. Validation tools route low-confidence results to human review, and integrations connect with robotic process automation, ERP, and content management systems. ABBYY has added generative AI features and tools for making documents ready for use by language models, as companies seek to feed documents into AI workflows.

item.title: ACE Studio
